old: Parliament had still not ratified the agreement at that point.
new: On 27 August 2026 the result was tabled in Papua New Guinea's parliament, and Prime Minister James Marape said the two governments would consult in October to set a date for the vote. Minister Manasseh Makiba said a yes vote would start a transitional self-government phase and would not bring immediate independence. The required majority is disputed: the PNG government says two-thirds or three-quarters of an absolute majority, the governing coalition has asked for 89 MPs, and the Bougainville government argues for 60 seats. AAP reports that Bougainville's leaders aim for greater self-government in September 2027 and full sovereignty in 2030, and that its government plans to declare sovereignty by 2030 if parliament delays further. No vote date had been reported in sources found by November 2026.

old: After the 2024 unrest, New Zealand's foreign minister questioned the vote's legitimacy, and France's ambassador to the Pacific criticised his remarks.
new: After the 2024 unrest, New Zealand's foreign minister questioned the vote's legitimacy, and France's ambassador to the Pacific criticised his remarks. Riots in May 2024 over plans to widen the frozen voter roll killed 14 people and caused over €2 billion in damage. The Bougival accord of 12 July 2025 and the Élysée-Oudinot accord of 19 January 2026 proposed a new status. The FLNKS withdrew its signature from Bougival, saying it had been misled, and boycotted the talks. On 2 April 2026 France's National Assembly rejected the constitutional bill without debate, 190 to 107, on a motion filed by Emmanuel Tjibaou. Delayed provincial elections on 28 June 2026 gave the pro-France bloc 24 of 54 Congress seats, pro-independence parties 26 and Éveil Océanien 4. In July 2026 Congress elected the pro-France Virginie Ruffenach as president, 28 votes to 26. The long-term status was left to talks with the French government, with no date set at that point.
